Eve · Genesis 2:18 LSV

Who Did God Create Women to Be?

From The God Who Hears Her by Dr. Connie Champeon · 3 min read

And YHWH God says, “[It is] not good for the man to be alone; I make him a helper as his counterpart.” (Genesis 2:18 LSV)

In Genesis, the woman is created as an 'ezer kenegdo'—a "helper as his counterpart" (Genesis 2:18). The problem is the English word "helper" implies a hierarchy where the "helper" is subordinate to the one being helped. However, in the Hebrew Bible, ‛êzer is most frequently used to describe God (e.g. Psalm 121:1-2, "My help [‛êzer] comes from the Lord"). God is never humanity’s assistant! Sixteen times in the Old Testament the Hebrew word 'ezer' describes God Himself as a powerful rescuer and ally in times of desperate need. So, far from implying a lesser status, it is a term of great strength.

Then there is that other sticky term kə-neḡ-dō. In English Bibles, it is most commonly translated “suitable.” But it is not translated like that anywhere else in the Bible. In about 150 other occurrences, neged is a preposition of physical presence. It means "in front of," "in the sight of," "opposite to," or "face-to-face.” The reason translators drifted toward "suitable" (and the KJV’s archaic "meet") is functional rather than literal. Linguistically, they were trying to solve a puzzle: If the woman is "in front of" or "opposite" the man, what does that mean for their relationship? They interpreted "opposite" as "complementary" (like two halves of a whole). "Complementary" became "matching." "Matching" became "suitable." By the time it reached the 20th century, "suitable" had lost its punch and started to sound like "serviceable" or "handy," which is a far cry from the original Hebrew.

We women were never made to be like men; we were made to be their opposite. But looking at how the term is used in the Bible, “face-to-face” would be more consistent. This made things very uncomfortable when the Scripture was first translated into Western cultures. If the Hebrew says, "I will make a Power (ezer) that stands Face-to-Face (neged) with him," it sounds like the arrival of a peer-commander. It sounds nothing like a glorified housekeeper (which is of course obviously what God meant - sarcasm intended). When you read the first chapters of Genesis without domesticity in mind, God had a very different mission for both Adam and Eve. They weren't created to start a family and build a cozy home. They were created to push back the kingdom of darkness, to bring order to chaos and establish a beacon of light. Eve wasn't created for her domestic skills: she was created to bring to the battlefield what Adam lacked and because fighting a battle alone is always 100 times harder. She was there to help him figure out a battle plan and implement it, not to sit in the background and fix supper while he fought it out for himself.

But, frankly, in many ways the Western interpretation is easier and more comfortable for all of us. Some days it frustrates me, but many days I'd rather cook supper than wage war with my husband against the kingdom of darkness. (Naturally sometimes due to our family's tendency to struggle with ‘hangry,’ hunger+angry, fixing supper does both). It is easier to be passive, and it's certainly more comfortable than to put on my armor, pick up my sword, and march into the battle together. I think Satan has done a clever trick to convince half of God's army that they were never called to the battlefield or that their only battlefield is their family and home.
